alternate_names: the principle of the worst piece
knowledge_type_note: Typed a rule of thumb rather than a principle for a specific reason: both of its earliest formulations contain an explicit precondition, so the rule was never stated unconditionally by the people credited with it.

attributions.note: Credited by GM Serper as the first formulation, and it is the one that already contains the exception.
Calls it Makogonov's rule and supplies the Makogonov quotation.
The formulation most often quoted, with its precondition intact.
Calls it 'the principle of the worst piece'.
Botvinnik called it 'Fischer's rule', though Fischer never stated it - the association rests on his games rather than on anything he wrote.

history.notes: One rule, four names, and no settled attribution. Anderssen appears earliest, Makogonov supplies the standard wording, Dvoretsky supplies the standard name, and Botvinnik attached Fischer's name to a rule Fischer never stated. All five attributions reach this base through a single secondary source - a Chess.com article by GM Serper - and none has been verified at primary source, which is why the confidence is recorded as disputed rather than medium.

competing_claims.note: Serper's own view: 'I think the great Adolf Anderssen was first.'
Botvinnik's name for it, though Fischer never explicitly stated the rule.

competing_claims.claim: The principle of the worst piece

engine_era_note: Broadly confirmed in spirit - engines readily play quiet repositioning moves that improve the least active piece - but engines also expose the priority problem sharply, since they will abandon a piece-improvement plan instantly for a concrete idea a human would not see.

preconditions: No forcing sequence or urgent threat demands attention
One piece is clearly doing less than the others
indicators_for: A piece with no available useful squares
A piece blocking its own side's plan
A rook on a closed file with nothing to do
A bishop shut in behind its own pawns
indicators_against: The opponent has a concrete threat that must be met
A forcing line is available that decides matters
The opponent is building an initiative that a quiet move would concede
false_positive_traps: The rule's precondition is the load-bearing part and is usually dropped in quotation. Anderssen says 'unless you can derive immediate advantage by an attack' and Makogonov says 'in positions where no other important matters need to be considered'. Without those, it is not the rule they stated.
Improving pieces while the opponent builds an initiative produces individually reasonable moves and a collectively lost position. This is the commonest way the rule is misapplied.
Identifying the worst piece is a judgement, not a measurement. This system has no reliable detector for it and must not claim one.

typical_plans: Find the piece doing least and give it a route to a better square
Trade the worst piece for one of the opponent's best
Reposition rather than advance when the position offers no concrete target
typical_moves: Quiet rook lifts to a file that may open
Bishop redeployments along a longer diagonal
Knight manoeuvres of two or three moves towards an outpost
typical_piece_arrangements: A piece with no useful squares available
strategic_consequences: Positional strength accumulates through the least active piece, which is where the cheapest improvement lies

exceptions: Anderssen's own exception: when immediate advantage is available from an attack.
Makogonov's own precondition: only where no other important matters need consideration.
When the opponent has counterplay, quiet improvement concedes the initiative.
limitations: The rule does not establish priority, which is the hard part of positional play and what it is most often asked to supply.
Every attribution here rests on one secondary source and none is verified at primary source.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the first trap - Anderssen's 'unless you can derive immediate advantage by an attack' and Makogonov's 'in positions where no other important matters need to be considered' - is built as far as a static test reaches: the move must not be a capture or a check, the side must not be in check, and the position after it must leave the opponent no winning capture. What is NOT built is 'no other important matters', which is the judgement the record's third trap says this base must not claim, and it does not: it reports that a move raised the scope of the least active piece, at low confidence, and never which piece is worst.
misconceptions: That the rule is unconditional. Neither of its earliest formulations states it that way.
That the worst piece is always the one to move. It is the default when nothing else is asking to be done.
That Fischer formulated it. Botvinnik named it after him; Fischer never stated it.

conflicts.resolution: The rule yields. Both original formulations say so explicitly - Anderssen excepts an immediate attacking advantage and Makogonov requires that nothing more important is going on. Where the opponent has counterplay, spending moves on quiet improvement is how the advantage is lost.

by_level.beginner: If nothing urgent is happening, find the piece doing the least and give it something to do.
by_level.intermediate: Improve your worst-placed piece - or trade it for one of their good ones. Two solutions to the same problem.
by_level.advanced: Note the condition both original formulations carry: only when nothing more important is going on. The hard part is judging that.
by_level.master: The rule does not supply priority, which is precisely what it is usually asked for.

by_depth.short: When nothing urgent is happening, improve your worst piece.
by_depth.normal: Find the piece doing least and improve it - or exchange it for one of the opponent's best. It works because a position's strength is the sum of what its pieces do, so the cheapest improvement available is to the piece contributing least.
by_depth.deep: The most practical positional advice there is, and the one most often quoted without the condition its authors attached. Anderssen's version excepts the case where an attack yields immediate advantage; Makogonov's applies only 'in positions where no other important matters need to be considered'. The popular short form drops both, and the truncation is the source of the rule's commonest misuse - spending two or three moves improving pieces while the opponent builds an initiative, each move looking reasonable and the position already worse. The rule tells you what to do when nothing else is asking to be done; it does not tell you whether that is the case, and that judgement is the hard part of positional play.

explanations.hedge: Both original formulations are conditional, and the condition - that nothing more urgent is happening - is the part that decides whether the rule applies.
explanations.lesson: The rule is what to do when there is nothing to do. Deciding whether that is true is the real work.

advanced_words: the principle of the worst piece

definition_short: When nothing more urgent is happening, find your worst-placed piece and improve it.
definition_long:
The most practical piece of positional advice there is, and the one most often quoted without the condition its own authors attached to it.

THE RULE, in the two earliest formulations found here, both of which are conditional:
- ANDERSSEN: 'Move that one of your pieces, which is in the worst plight, UNLESS you can satisfy yourself that you can derive immediate advantage by an attack.'
- MAKOGONOV, as quoted by Mikhalchishin: 'IN POSITIONS WHERE NO OTHER IMPORTANT MATTERS NEED TO BE CONSIDERED, one should identify one's worst-placed piece and bring it to a more active square.'
Both carry the exception inside the statement. The popular short form — 'improve your worst piece' — is a truncation, and this base treats the truncation as the source of the rule's most common misuse.

WHY IT WORKS is that a position's strength is the sum of what its pieces are doing, so the cheapest available improvement is almost always to the piece doing least. It also turns positional play from something mysterious into something procedural: instead of searching for a plan, look for the unhappiest piece.

THE FAILURE MODE is priority, not correctness. A position usually contains several valid ideas at once, and improving pieces for two or three moves while the opponent builds an initiative elsewhere produces moves that each look reasonable and a position that is already worse. Principles do not establish which factor dominates — that is exactly what the preconditions in Anderssen's and Makogonov's own wordings are there to guard.

THE EXCHANGE COROLLARY is worth having alongside it: trade your worst pieces for the opponent's best. Improving a bad piece and trading it off are two solutions to the same problem.
